title: How to Get Mortgage Free Like Me: Real Aussies Reveal How They've Done It Faster, Smarter and Cheaper
author: Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon
summary:
*How to Get Mortgage Free Like Me* is Australian finance journalist Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon's practical guide to paying off a home loan faster and more cheaply, built around her own experience clearing her mortgage in seven years and combined with real case studies from other Australian families who did the same. The book is aimed squarely at ordinary homeowners rather than property investors, and its core message is that most people are structurally overpaying on their home loan without realizing it, simply because banks aren't incentivized to volunteer the tricks that would shrink the interest bill.

The book's most emphasized tool is the offset account — a transaction account linked to a mortgage whose balance reduces the interest charged on the loan without actually paying down the loan principal, preserving flexibility to access the money later while still cutting interest costs. Pedersen-McKinnon walks through multiple ways to maximize an offset account's effect, including directing savings and even everyday spending through it strategically, and using it in combination with a long-interest-free-period credit card so more cash sits in the offset for longer before bills are due — a specific micro-repayment tactic she presents as one of the highest-leverage, lowest-effort tricks in the book.

Woven throughout are real stories from Australian families with different starting incomes, family situations, and property types, used to demonstrate that the strategies are broadly applicable rather than only available to high earners. The book balances motivational, first-person storytelling with concrete numbers — showing, for a given loan size, how much interest and time can be saved by specific combinations of the tactics covered.

Later sections extend beyond the core home mortgage into related debt situations: managing a second or third property purchase, consolidating higher-interest debts into cheaper mortgage-linked structures, and other more complex strategies for households further along in their financial journey, while keeping the practical, numbers-forward tone established in the earlier chapters.

sections.title: The Credit Card and Offset Trick
sections.summary:
This tactic involves routing regular monthly expenses through a credit card with a long interest-free period, while leaving the equivalent cash sitting in the offset account until the credit card bill is actually due.
The section walks through the mechanics with concrete numbers, showing meaningfully increased interest savings and a shortened payoff timeline compared to not using the trick.
It hands off into the real-family case studies that follow, showing the tactic applied to different actual households.
keyLessons: Timing cash flow between an offset account and a long-interest-free credit card can meaningfully increase total interest savings.
Small, consistent micro-repayment tactics compound into a materially shorter loan term over years.

whoThisIsFor: Australian homeowners with a standard home loan looking for practical, numbers-based strategies to pay it off faster, rather than property investors or readers outside Australia's specific mortgage product landscape.
whenToReadThis: Early in a home loan term, when structural changes (like adding an offset account) have the most years left to compound their benefit.

authorBio.name: Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon
authorBio.bio:
Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is an Australian financial journalist and money commentator, known for a long-running personal-finance column and frequent television appearances discussing household money management, mortgages, and consumer finance. She has built a public reputation specifically around practical, everyday money advice for ordinary Australian households rather than institutional investing.

Her own experience paying off her home loan in seven years is a recurring credibility anchor across her media appearances and this book specifically, which she wrote to share both her own tactics and the real experiences of other Australian families who achieved similar results.
notableWorks: (primarily known for this title and ongoing financial journalism/columns rather than a large additional book catalog)

conceptsFrameworks.name: Offset Account Leverage
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The book's central financial tool: a transaction account linked to a mortgage whose balance directly reduces the interest charged, without reducing the loan principal, allowing a homeowner to cut interest costs while retaining access to their money for flexibility.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: The Offset Account as a "Mortgage-Busting Secret Weapon"

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Credit Card–Offset Micro-Repayment Trick
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A specific tactic of routing routine monthly spending through a long-interest-free-period credit card while keeping the equivalent cash in an offset account until the bill is due, increasing the average balance sitting in the offset and therefore increasing total interest savings over the life of the loan.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: The Credit Card and Offset Trick

actionSteps: Check whether your current mortgage has an offset account feature, and if not, look into whether your lender offers one or whether refinancing to one makes sense for your loan size.
Redirect any spare cash you currently hold in a low-interest savings account into your mortgage offset account instead.
If you have a low-interest-free-period-eligible credit card, trial routing one month of routine expenses through it while keeping the equivalent cash in your offset until the statement is due.
Run the actual numbers (loan balance, interest rate, current offset balance) to calculate your specific potential interest savings from increasing your offset balance.
reflectionQuestions: How much of your current cash flow is sitting in low-interest accounts instead of working against your mortgage interest through an offset?
What's stopping you from applying the credit-card-and-offset trick right now — unfamiliarity, discipline, or your current bank's account structure?
If mortgage freedom is achievable through structural choices rather than a higher income, which structural choice have you not yet made?

points: Much of the book's numeric advantage comes from Australia's specific offset-account mortgage product structure, which isn't universally available in the same form in other countries, limiting the direct portability of the core tactic for non-Australian readers.

The credit-card-and-offset trick requires real financial discipline (paying the card off in full every cycle); if a reader carries a balance instead, the interest charged on the credit card would likely outweigh any offset benefit, a risk the book's framing doesn't heavily emphasize in the promotional material.

The strategies were written and case-studied in a specific low-interest-rate Australian mortgage environment; the size of the savings shown in examples would shift meaningfully in a higher-interest-rate environment, which is worth checking against current rates rather than the book's original figures.
As with many "everyday Aussie case study" finance books, the featured families may not be fully representative of households with less financial flexibility or more precarious income.
criticalTake.contextNote: Australian mortgage interest rates have moved significantly since the book's original release, so readers should recalculate the specific dollar-savings examples in the book against current rates rather than assuming the original figures still apply directly.
